title: The 3 Pillars of Autonomy – Michele Catasta, Replit
talk_summary: Replit's agent lead argues autonomy should be scoped, not measured by long runtimes, and rests on three pillars: frontier model capability, in-loop verification, and context management. The most concrete mechanisms are autonomous browser testing via generated Playwright code (an order of magnitude cheaper/faster than computer-use), sub-agent orchestration to isolate context, and core-loop-driven parallelism.

takeaways.technique: Generate Playwright tests as reusable regression suite instead of computer-use
takeaways.what_they_do: Rather than exposing generic browser tools (click/fill) to the agent, they have the agent write Playwright code directly, which is expressive, LLM-friendly, and reusable as a regression suite; screenshots/computer-use only as fallback.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we directly write playrite code ... the moment you created a test you're also creating a regression test suite
takeaways.numbers: roughly an order of magnitude cheaper and faster compared to computer use; >30% of individual features broken on first generation

takeaways.technique: Sub-agents with fresh context for verification
takeaways.what_they_do: Verification runs in a sub-agent invoked from the core loop with a minimal injected context; its context is discarded and only the final observation returns to the main loop, avoiding context pollution.
takeaways.evidence_quote: We make this happen all within a sub agent. Then we scratch the context window of that sub agent. We just return back the last observation
takeaways.numbers: memories per compression went from ~35 to ~45-50

takeaways.technique: Offload state to filesystem/codebase instead of context window
takeaways.what_they_do: Persist plans, task lists, docs, and memories to the file system and let the agent read/write them when relevant, keeping working context under ~200k tokens even for long tasks.
takeaways.evidence_quote: most of the tasks, even the more ambitious one, can be accomplished within the 200,000 tokens

takeaways.technique: Core loop as orchestrator for parallelism (not user-decomposed)
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of the user manually splitting tasks into parallel threads and resolving merge conflicts, the main agent loop decomposes tasks and decides parallelism on the fly, choosing subtasks that avoid stepping on each other.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the subtask that we're going to be working on are not determined by the user but they're determined by the corion loop

takeaways.technique: In-loop verification to counter model 'laziness'/false completion claims
takeaways.what_they_do: They don't trust a model's claim that a task is done; verification steps check actual behavior (DB reads, logs, API calls, clicks) to confirm results aren't hallucinated.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we need to verify that whenever a model tells us that a task has been completed, there is actually the truth

takeaways.technique: Parallelism trades compute for latency; sample multiple trajectories
takeaways.what_they_do: They accept extra compute (shared ~80% context duplicated across parallel agents) to cut wall-clock time and optionally sample multiple trajectories for better results.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you trade off basically extra compute in exchange for time
